text.hook:
Two overloads, each with `class = enable_if_t<...>`.
Different conditions. The compiler sees one template, defined twice.

Swipe ➜ from SFINAE to concepts, plus 6 myths that fail interviews.
text.body:
Inside:
1. Three generations of constraints
2. What SFINAE does and does not catch
3. enable_if forms and traps
4. if constexpr limits
5. Concepts, requires and subsumption
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.hero:
SFINAE to concepts:
the constraint toolbox
+ 6 myths
slides.lead: enable_if, void_t, tag dispatch, if constexpr, requires and subsumption.

slides.title: Three generations, all still in use
slides.takeaway: All compile time, zero runtime cost. Type traits are the shared vocabulary.

slides.title: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error

cards.label: Removed
cards.text: Invalid type or expression in the **signature** after substituting `T`: the overload silently drops out.

cards.label: Hard error
cards.text: Errors in the **body**, in a trait's own definition, or in `noexcept(...)`.

cards.label: `auto` return
cards.text: Signature is just `auto`: it stays viable and the body fails hard.

slides.takeaway: Put the check in the signature or in a constraint, never only in the body.

slides.title: Forms and traps
items: Preferred: `std::enable_if_t<C, int> = 0` as a template parameter
`class = enable_if_t<C>` twice: **redefinition** (defaults are not the signature)
Return-type form `enable_if_t<C, R> f(T)`: no use for constructors
slides.takeaway: C++20: a `requires` clause replaces most `enable_if` code.

slides.title: The discarded branch

cards.label: Skipped
cards.text: Inside a template, with a condition that depends on `T`, the discarded branch is not instantiated.

cards.label: Return deduction
cards.text: `return` statements in a discarded branch do not take part in return type deduction.

cards.label: static_assert(false)
cards.text: GCC 11 rejects it. P2593 (C++23, a DR): GCC 13+ accepts.

slides.takeaway: Portable old trick for the assert: `static_assert(always_false<T>)`.

slides.title: Four kinds of requirement
slides.takeaway: A requires-expression is itself a `bool` constant expression.

slides.title: How concepts are ordered

cards.label: Ordering
cards.text: A constrained template beats an unconstrained one. `A && B` subsumes `A`.

cards.label: By identity
cards.text: Atomic constraints compare by **source location**, not meaning.

cards.label: So
cards.text: Two inline `is_integral_v<T>`: ambiguous. Named concepts: resolved.

slides.takeaway: Build constraints from named concepts and reuse them.

items.myth: "Any error during overload resolution is SFINAE."
items.truth: Only failures in the immediate context of the signature.

items.myth: "Two overloads with `class = enable_if_t<...>` defaults are fine."
items.truth: Redefinition: defaults are not the signature. Use `enable_if_t<C, int> = 0`.
They only choose which template is used. No run-time cost.

items.myth: "`static_assert(false)` in an `if constexpr` else is always an error."
items.truth: Accepted since P2593 (GCC 13+). Older compilers need a dependent `false`.
Only in unevaluated contexts (`decltype`, `sizeof`). Evaluated use fails to compile.

items.myth: "Concepts with the same meaning subsume each other."
items.truth: Subsumption compares atomic constraints by source identity.

slides.hero:
Constrain at the call site.
Name your concepts.
Reuse them.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
A special print for floating point, enable_if guarded.
A generic print for everything else.
Classic SFINAE. Ship it?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Two calls: one int, one double.

slides.title: What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC: call of overloaded 'print(double)' is ambiguous
bullets: `print(7)`: SFINAE removes the `enable_if` overload. Only the generic one is viable: fine.
`print(2.5)`: both are viable, both take a `double`.
Partial ordering compares parameter types only. The `enable_if` condition is not part of it.
slides.wrong: "A: the constrained overload is more specialized"

slides.title: A concept, which does take part in ordering
slides.tip: Pre-C++20: add `enable_if_t<!is_floating_point_v<T>, int> = 0` to the generic one.
slides.takeaway: SFINAE only removes candidates. It never makes one better.

text.hook:
A C++20 concept for types bigger than 4 bytes.
Is char Big? Is double?
Two versions, one keyword apart.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Each concept is tested with char (1 byte) and double (8 bytes on x86-64).

slides.title: What does this print?

slides.verdict_sub: `Big<char>` is true: the size is never tested
bullets: `Big` uses a **simple requirement**: it checks that `sizeof(T) > 4` is a valid expression.
For `char` it is valid (and false), so the concept is satisfied.
`ReallyBig` uses a **nested requirement**, which checks that the value is `true`.
slides.wrong: "B: Big<char> is false because sizeof(char) is 1"

slides.title: Say what you mean
slides.tip: Inside `requires { }` only a nested `requires` tests a value. Everything else tests validity.
slides.takeaway: A simple requirement asks "does it compile?", not "is it true?".

text.hook:
Only process<int> is ever called.
The else branch of if constexpr is discarded.
So its broken code never compiles. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: There are two suspicious calls in the else branch. Only one of them matters.

slides.title: Does this compile?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC: request for member 'size' in 'counter', which is of non-class type 'int'
bullets: `v.name()` depends on `T`: in the discarded branch it is never instantiated. No error.
`counter` is always an `int`: not dependent. It is checked when the template is defined (phase 1).
slides.wrong: "A: the else branch is thrown away"

slides.title: Only dependent code is skipped
slides.tip: Outside a template, `if constexpr` discards nothing for checking: both branches must compile.
slides.takeaway: `if constexpr` hides only code that depends on `T`.

text.hook:
check(x) with int x.
Is T int? Is T integral?
Ask any engineer and they say yes, twice.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: One forwarding reference, three calls, three type traits each.

slides.title: What does this print?

bullets: Forwarding reference: an lvalue `int` deduces `T = int&`, a const lvalue `T = const int&`.
Only the rvalue `3` deduces plain `T = int`.
`is_integral_v<int&>` is false: a reference is not an integral type.

slides.title: Strip the reference first
slides.tip: Same trap: `is_const_v<const int&>` is false. A reference itself is never const.
slides.takeaway: Ask traits about `remove_cvref_t<T>`, not a forwarded `T`.
